slides.title: Implementation Issues
slides.notes: Open by framing the chapter as the moment where geometric algebra becomes software. The earlier chapters made objects feel coordinate-free, but a program must still choose slots, signs, metrics, tests, and kernels. The promise is practical: representation choices should preserve the geometry while making later algorithms inspectable.

slides.title: Four Implementation Levels
slides.notes: Use the four levels as a mental stack. Basis blades decide names and products, linear multivectors decide coordinate storage and distributive loops, nonlinear algorithms handle operations that need specialized numerical work, and applications should see stable geometric operations rather than raw storage details.

slides.title: Basis Ordering Contract
slides.notes: Pause on the basis order because every downstream table, array, and generated kernel inherits it. A bit mask is compact, but it is not self-explanatory unless the implementation fixes the basis-vector order, grade ordering, and slot names before any product table is trusted.

slides.title: Product Signs And Metrics
slides.notes: Walk through the product as three separate concerns: the surviving basis-vector set, the parity sign from reordering, and the metric factor from repeated vectors. Separating these concerns helps students debug signs without confusing orientation errors with signature-dependent metric behavior.

slides.title: Dense Coordinates
slides.notes: Dense coordinates are attractive because the array shape is fixed and every operation has an obvious loop. The important warning is that fixed shape is not the same as efficient shape. In high dimension, most geometric objects touch only a small fraction of the available slots.

slides.title: Sparse And Factored Forms
slides.notes: Contrast sparse maps with factored blades as two ways of refusing to pay for unused coordinates. Sparse coordinates keep the additive basis-blade language, while factored blades keep the generating vectors. Each representation makes one class of operations pleasant and another class more expensive.

slides.title: Matrix Representations
slides.notes: Treat matrices as a verification tool and a narrow implementation option, not as a replacement for the geometric interface. Matrix multiplication can model the geometric product in small Clifford algebras, but grade projection, outer product, contractions, and model predicates still need explicit attention.

slides.title: Symbolic Bootstrap
slides.notes: Position symbolic algebra as a development-time assistant. It can derive coordinate formulas, expose sign conventions, and generate specialized code, but the runtime path should usually be numeric. The useful workflow is derive, freeze, test, and then execute a compact kernel repeatedly.

slides.title: Validation Ladder
slides.notes: Make testing feel structural rather than anecdotal. A few hand products are necessary, but the reliable implementation checks entire layers: basis table consistency, dense and sparse agreement, matrix representation preservation, nonlinear residuals, and application-level geometric invariants.

slides.title: Performance Tradeoffs
slides.notes: The chart is not meant to settle the representation question by itself. It gives the class a scale sense: full multivectors grow exponentially, fixed grades grow combinatorially, and factored blades grow with the number of stored vectors. Real performance also depends on memory layout and specialization.

slides.title: Representation Policy
slides.notes: Use the policy slide as a decision exercise. Ask what the algorithm actually touches, whether products preserve sparsity, whether grade information matters, and whether the implementation will be run once for derivation or millions of times in an application loop.

slides.title: Part III Roadmap
slides.notes: Connect the chapter to the rest of the part. Chapter 18 names the implementation questions, Chapter 19 makes basis blades reliable, Chapter 20 distributes linear products, Chapter 21 treats nonlinear operations as algorithms, Chapter 22 specializes performance, and Chapter 23 tests the stack in application code.

slides.title: Carry Forward
slides.notes: Close by making the main habit explicit: do not choose a representation only because it is elegant on paper. Choose it because it keeps the required products, signs, metrics, validations, and performance profile visible enough that the geometric code remains trustworthy.
